text: This lesson goes beyond the basic role inheritance you already know, into actually designing a role hierarchy on purpose — least privilege, narrow custom roles, and the real risk of role sprawl.

Quick recap: a role lives in sys_user_role, and its Contains Roles field lists other roles it inherits from. Grant someone itil_admin, and they automatically inherit everything itil grants, plus more. System Administration's Roles & Role Inheritance lesson already covered that mechanic. This lesson is about something different: designing that hierarchy deliberately, instead of just understanding the one you're handed.

Least privilege means granting the minimum access a person actually needs, nothing more. Delegated Administration already applied this to one specific case — a help-desk delegate who only resets passwords. This lesson generalizes that same discipline to every role grant: ask what this person needs to do today, then build a role that grants exactly that, and nothing else.

Out-of-box roles like admin and itil_admin are convenient, not correctly scoped. Reaching for admin because it's easier than thinking through the actual need creates a role nobody can audit. Building a narrow custom role instead — one you can describe in a single sentence, like 'this lets someone reassign incidents, full stop' — takes more thought up front, but that thought is the entire point.

Role sprawl is the real risk: narrow roles built correctly, one at a time, pile up over years into dozens of overlapping custom roles with tangled inheritance chains nobody fully understands anymore. Each individual decision felt safer than reusing a broader existing role. Without a periodic review of the whole hierarchy — consolidating overlap, retiring roles nobody uses — that accumulated complexity itself becomes the security risk, independent of whether any single role was ever misconfigured.

Next, the Security Model Lab walks through exactly this scenario: auditing a real company's three years of accumulated, overlapping facilities roles, and redesigning them into a clean, least-privilege hierarchy.
